title: The Adrenal Axis
rationale: Your highest-volume weakness: 47% across 17 questions. The recorded misses show one principle failing repeatedly across three different diseases — renin direction misread in Addison's, Conn's, and renal artery stenosis.
objectives: Use renin, not aldosterone, as the discriminator between primary and secondary aldosteronism, and explain why aldosterone alone carries no information.
Predict the electrolyte and glucose pattern of cortisol excess versus cortisol deficiency, in both directions.
Distinguish primary from secondary adrenal insufficiency using ACTH and the aldosterone/renin pair, and explain why aldosterone is spared in secondary disease.
Recognise adrenal crisis and state the immediate management, including why fludrocortisone is not part of it.
Apply the sick-day rules and explain when doubling oral steroid is no longer sufficient.
Interpret a short Synacthen test against current Australian thresholds.

sections.heading: The one rule that fixes most of these questions
sections.body:
**Aldosterone is high in both primary and secondary aldosteronism. It tells you nothing on its own. Renin decides.**

| | Renin | Aldosterone | ARR | Where the problem is |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Primary (Conn's)** | **Low/suppressed** | High | **High** | The adrenal — autonomous secretion |
| **Secondary (e.g. renal artery stenosis)** | **High** | High | Normal | Upstream — something is driving RAAS |
| **Addison's** | **High** | **Low** | — | The gland has failed entirely |

The logic: in Conn's the adrenal secretes autonomously, volume expands, and feedback **switches renin off**. If renin is high, something upstream is driving the system — a stenotic renal artery, heart failure, cirrhosis, or hypovolaemia.

Read renin first, every time.

sections.heading: Cortisol excess versus deficiency — learn it in both directions
sections.body:
| | Cortisol EXCESS (Cushing's) | Cortisol DEFICIENCY (Addison's) |
|---|---|---|
| Potassium | **Low** | **High** |
| Sodium | Normal/high | **Low** |
| Bicarbonate | **High** (alkalosis) | Low (acidosis) |
| Glucose | **High** | **Low** |
| BP | **High** | **Low**, postural |

Cortisol is catabolic and insulin-antagonistic, so excess raises glucose. At very high concentrations it saturates 11β-HSD2 and spills onto mineralocorticoid receptors — hence hypokalaemia and alkalosis in ectopic ACTH.

Deficiency inverts all of it. Hyponatraemia has two mechanisms worth separating: **aldosterone deficiency** causes salt wasting (primary only), while **loss of cortisol's suppression of ADH** causes water retention (both primary and secondary). That is why **hyponatraemia occurs in both, but hyperkalaemia only in primary** — potassium needs aldosterone to be gone.

sections.heading: Primary versus secondary adrenal insufficiency
sections.body:
The adrenal cortex has three layers, and **they are not all controlled by ACTH**:

| Layer | Product | Driven by |
|---|---|---|
| Zona **g**lomerulosa | Aldosterone (**salt**) | **RAAS — not ACTH** |
| Zona **f**asciculata | Cortisol (**sugar**) | ACTH |
| Zona **r**eticularis | Androgens (**sex**) | ACTH |

*Salt, sugar, sex — the deeper you go, the sweeter it gets.*

That single fact generates the discriminator:

| | Primary (Addison's) | Secondary (pituitary/steroid withdrawal) |
|---|---|---|
| **ACTH** | **High** | **Low or inappropriately normal** |
| **Aldosterone** | **Low** | **Normal** — RAAS is intact |
| **Renin** | **High** | Normal |
| **Potassium** | **High** | **Normal** |
| Pigmentation | **Yes** (ACTH/MSH share POMC) | **No** |

Secondary spares the zona glomerulosa because aldosterone never depended on ACTH. This is why a symptomatic, hypotensive patient with a **normal potassium** almost certainly does not have established primary disease.

**Commonest cause of secondary AI: abrupt withdrawal of long-term exogenous corticosteroid.** The axis is suppressed and the cortex atrophies from disuse.

sections.heading: Adrenal crisis and the sick-day rules
sections.body:
**Adrenal crisis** — hypotension and shock, often with vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, fever, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia. Typically precipitated by infection, surgery, trauma, or missed doses.

**Immediate management:**

1. **IV/IM hydrocortisone 100mg stat** — do not wait for confirmatory cortisol or ACTH
2. **Aggressive IV 0.9% saline**
3. Correct hypoglycaemia
4. Treat the precipitant

**Fludrocortisone has no role acutely.** At stress doses, hydrocortisone supplies ample mineralocorticoid activity — roughly 40mg of hydrocortisone is equivalent to a usual daily fludrocortisone dose. Uptitrating fludrocortisone in a crisis is a distractor.

**Sick-day rules:**

- **Rule 1** — fever or intercurrent illness: **double** the oral hydrocortisone until recovered
- **Rule 2** — vomiting, diarrhoea, or unable to absorb: **switch to IM hydrocortisone** and seek urgent help

The trap: once a patient is vomiting, doubling the *oral* dose is no longer an option. Every patient should carry an emergency injection kit and a steroid alert card.

**Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2 (Schmidt)** — autoimmune thyroid disease plus Addison's ± type 1 diabetes. Any patient with one organ-specific autoimmune endocrinopathy is at risk of another, so Hashimoto's in the stem is a clue, not background noise.

sections.heading: Short Synacthen test — Australian thresholds
sections.body:
250 mcg Synacthen, cortisol measured at baseline and 30 minutes.

- **Pass ≈ >430 nmol/L at 30 min** (PathWest), or **>500 nmol/L at 60 min**. Many labs use **>450 nmol/L** to exclude; **350–449** is borderline
- Older texts quote **550 nmol/L** — a deliberately conservative cutoff from older assays. Modern assays put the lower normal limit closer to **418–469**
- The figure is **assay-dependent**, which is exactly why a well-written exam question gives you the reference range

**Supporting tests:**

| Test | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| 9am cortisol <100 nmol/L | Strongly suggests adrenal insufficiency |
| 9am cortisol >300–400 nmol/L | Effectively excludes it; Synacthen not needed |
| ACTH high (often >200 ng/L) | **Primary** |
| ACTH low/normal (<10 ng/L) | **Secondary** |
| Aldosterone low + renin high | **Primary** |

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman has fatigue, weight loss and postural hypotension. Na 129, K 5.7, glucose 3.4.
questions.explanation: Low sodium, high potassium, low glucose and hypotension is cortisol (and aldosterone) deficiency. Cortisol excess would give the exact inversion: low K, high glucose, hypertension. Learning the pattern in both directions is what makes this fast.

questions.stem: A patient with known Addison's disease develops influenza with a fever of 38.5°C. She is eating and drinking normally and not vomiting.
questions.lead: What should she do with her hydrocortisone?
options: Double the usual oral dose until she recovers
Stop it until the fever settles
questions.explanation: Sick-day rule 1: double the oral dose for fever or intercurrent illness. She is tolerating oral intake, so IM is not yet required — that is rule 2, for vomiting, diarrhoea, or failure to absorb. Stopping steroid in illness risks precipitating crisis.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman has resistant hypertension and K 3.0. Plasma aldosterone is elevated and plasma renin activity is suppressed.
questions.explanation: High aldosterone with suppressed renin is primary aldosteronism — the adrenal is secreting autonomously, and the resulting volume expansion switches renin off. If renin were high, something upstream would be driving RAAS, pointing to a secondary cause such as renal artery stenosis.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man on prednisolone 15mg daily for 10 months for polymyalgia rheumatica stops it abruptly. Four days later he is fatigued and hypotensive. Na 132, K 4.1, glucose 3.3. There is no hyperpigmentation.
questions.lead: Which set of results do you expect?
options: ACTH high, aldosterone low, renin high
ACTH low, aldosterone normal, renin normal
ACTH high, aldosterone normal, renin normal
ACTH low, aldosterone low, renin high
questions.explanation: This is secondary adrenal insufficiency from abrupt withdrawal of exogenous steroid. The pituitary is suppressed → ACTH low. But aldosterone is ACTH-independent — the zona glomerulosa runs on RAAS, so aldosterone and renin stay normal, which is exactly why his potassium is normal (4.1) and he has no pigmentation. Contrast with primary disease, where the whole cortex fails.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with known peripheral vascular disease has hypertension and K 2.6. Renin activity is raised, aldosterone is raised, and the aldosterone/renin ratio is normal. A left renal bruit is audible.
options: Renal artery stenosis with secondary aldosteronism
questions.explanation: Both renin and aldosterone raised with a normal ratio = secondary aldosteronism. Reduced renal perfusion drives renin → angiotensin II → aldosterone, causing hypokalaemia and hypertension. Conn's requires suppressed renin and a high ratio. The bruit and vascular history point to the renal artery as the upstream driver.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with Hashimoto's thyroiditis presents with vomiting, abdominal pain and confusion during a urinary tract infection. BP 80/48, Na 125, K 6.2, glucose 2.7. She has buccal pigmentation.
options: Await a random cortisol and ACTH before treating
questions.explanation: Adrenal crisis — treat immediately with IV hydrocortisone and aggressive saline; do not wait for confirmatory results. Buccal pigmentation indicates primary disease, and Hashimoto's suggests autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2. The UTI is the precipitant and needs treating, but not before the steroid and fluids. Fludrocortisone is redundant at stress-dose hydrocortisone.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected adrenal insufficiency has a short Synacthen test: baseline cortisol 210 nmol/L, 30-minute cortisol 390 nmol/L. The laboratory reference for an adequate response is >430 nmol/L at 30 minutes.
options: Inadequate response — adrenal insufficiency is present
questions.explanation: The 30-minute value of 390 falls below the stated threshold of 430, so the response is inadequate and adrenal insufficiency is confirmed. The increment is irrelevant — it is the absolute peak that matters. Note the question supplies the reference range, which is how a fair exam handles an assay-dependent cutoff. ACTH then localises: high = primary, low = secondary.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with small cell lung cancer develops hypertension, proximal weakness and oedema over 8 weeks. K 2.7, bicarbonate 33, glucose 13.4. He is not cushingoid in appearance.
questions.lead: What explains the hypokalaemia and alkalosis?
options: Aldosterone excess from an adrenal adenoma
Very high cortisol saturating 11β-HSD2 and acting on mineralocorticoid receptors
questions.explanation: Ectopic ACTH from small cell lung cancer produces extremely high cortisol, which overwhelms 11β-HSD2 (the enzyme that normally inactivates cortisol in the kidney), letting cortisol act on mineralocorticoid receptors → hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis, plus hyperglycaemia from cortisol's insulin antagonism. The rapid course means classic Cushingoid features have not had time to develop — weakness, oedema and hypertension dominate.

questions.stem: A patient presents collapsed with hypotension. Na 130, K 4.0, glucose 2.9. There is no hyperpigmentation. He takes no regular medications and has no known endocrine disease.
questions.lead: Which finding would most strongly argue AGAINST established primary adrenal insufficiency?
questions.explanation: Normal potassium is the mechanistically incompatible finding. Primary disease destroys the whole cortex including the zona glomerulosa, so aldosterone is lost and potassium must rise. Hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia occur in both primary and secondary disease (cortisol deficiency), so neither discriminates. Absent pigmentation is suggestive but weaker — it takes months to develop, so early primary disease may have none.

questions.stem: A patient in adrenal crisis has received IV hydrocortisone 100mg and 2L of saline. He improves. The intern asks whether fludrocortisone should now be added, given his aldosterone deficiency.
options: Yes — but only at double the usual dose
No — stress-dose hydrocortisone provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity
No — fludrocortisone is contraindicated in adrenal insufficiency
questions.explanation: At stress doses, hydrocortisone itself has substantial mineralocorticoid activity — roughly 40mg of hydrocortisone approximates a usual daily fludrocortisone dose, so at 100mg it is redundant. Fludrocortisone is resumed later as the hydrocortisone dose is weaned back to maintenance. It is not contraindicated — it is simply unnecessary right now, which makes option 4 wrong for a different reason than option 1.
